div.head: EGu 7.2
div.ab: Gif hlaford his þeowan freolsdæge nyde to weorce, gylde lahslitte inne on Deone lage ⁊ wíte mid Englum.
Gyf hlaford his ðeowan freolsdæge nyde to weorce, gylde lahslitte se hlaford inne on Dæne lage ⁊ wite mid Englum.
Si dominus seruum suum diebus festis cogat operari, reddat dominus ipse lahslit cum Dacis et witam cum Anglis.
Gif hlaford his þeowan freolsdæge nyde to weorce, gylde lahslitte [se hlaford] inne on Deone lage ⁊ wíte mid Englum.
Gif hlaford his þeowan freolsdæge nyde to weorce, gylde lahslitte se hlaford inne on Deone lage and wite mid Englum.
Wenn ein Herr am Feiertage seinen Sklaven zur Arbeit zwingt, zahle er (der Herr) Rechtsbruchbusse im Rechtsgebiet der Dänen und Strafgeld bei den Engländern.
If a lord forces his slave to work on a feast-day, let him (the lord) pay the penalty for breach of law within the Danelaw and a fine among the English.
If a slave is compelled to work by his lord during a church festival, he [the lord] shall pay lahslit within the Danelagh, and a fine in an English district.
If a master compels his slave to work on a holy day, he must pay lahslit within the Danelaw and a penalty among the English.

se hlaford, obwohl zum Sinne nicht notwendig, scheint laut des Hss.-Verhältnisses archetyp, vielleicht einst Randglosse. — Das ‘Dänen-Rechtsgebiet’ bed., genau ebenso wie mid Denum in diesem Denkmal, da es nur für Ostanglien gilt: ‘in den von Dänischem Recht beherrschten Gerichtsbezirken Ostangliens’

se hlaford, although not necessary to the sense, appears from the relationship of the MSS to belong to the archetype, perhaps originally a marginal gloss. — The ‘legal district of the Danes’ means, exactly like mid Denum in this text, since it applies only to East Anglia: ‘in the judicial districts of East Anglia governed by Danish law’

The Danelagh was the region within which Danish Law prevailed (cf. O. Norse Gulaþings Lög, Frostaþings Lög, etc., which denote not only the Laws of the Gulaþing and Frostaþing, etc., but also the districts within which these laws were enforced). The reference here, no doubt, is to the Danish kingdom of East Anglia, though elsewhere the term embraces other parts of England which were occupied by Danes (cf. Chadwick, Anglo-Saxon Institutions, p. 198 f.).
